1261.title: The setting sun
1261.hook: the first visualization: the setting sun, like a drum hung in the west
1261.howItsDone: Following the meditation sutra, some Pure Land practitioners sit facing west at sunset and hold the image of the setting sun in mind; in Japanese this is called nissokan, the sun contemplation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Queen Vaidehi in her locked room, asking for a land without sorrow, and then how to see it. Your line: a land without sorrow.

How do I see it? That was the queen's question, and it's a hard one. The land of bliss lies in the west, and nobody can walk there or look there. So the Buddha's first answer is almost startling in how plain it is. No chant. No doctrine. No secret. He tells her to look at something anyone can see on a clear evening: the sun, going down in the west.
screen: `HOW DO I SEE IT?` → `NO CHANT, NO SECRET.` → `THE SETTING SUN.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In the meditation sutra, the Buddha tells Vaidehi to sit facing west and look at the sun as it's about to set. Fix the mind on it, he says, steadily, without letting the thought wander anywhere else. Second, the image. As the sun sinks, the sutra says, it looks like a drum hanging in the sky: round, full, still, hung in the west. Then the real work: hold that image clear, whether the eyes are open or closed. The sunset ends. The drum stays. The sutra calls this the first meditation, the perception of the sun. Third, why the sun. Every evening the setting sun points west, toward the land of bliss. So the first step toward a land no one can see starts from the one thing anyone can see. In Japanese this practice is called nissokan, the sun contemplation. Fourth, where it leads. The sun is only the first rung of a ladder. The meditations that follow climb, one image at a time, from things the eyes know toward the land itself, and toward Amitabha. Each image steadies the mind enough to hold the next. Tomorrow's rung is water. For today, the whole practice fits in one evening: a window facing west, and a sun hung like a drum, held in mind after the light is gone.
screen: `SIT FACING WEST.` · `A DRUM HANGING IN THE SKY.` · `THE ONE THING ANYONE CAN SEE.` · `THE FIRST RUNG OF A LADDER.` · then, large: `THE DRUM IN THE WEST.`

segments.voice: If the sun is setting where you are, turn toward it without staring straight into it; if not, close your eyes and call up a sunset you remember. Let the sun hang low and round in the west like a drum, and when the image fades or the mind drifts, gently bring the drum back. Nothing to add, nothing to figure out.
The setting sun. The first meditation given to Queen Vaidehi: sit facing west, look at the sinking sun like a drum hung in the sky, and hold the image with eyes open or closed. Today's word.
Your line: the drum in the west. The light goes; the image stays. See you tomorrow.

1262.title: Water and ice
1262.hook: the visualizations continue: water, ice, crystal ground
1262.howItsDone: Some Pure Land practitioners work through the Contemplation Sutra's visualizations in order, from the setting sun to water, ice and the jewel ground; others center their practice on calling Amitabha's name and know the visualizations through reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the setting sun: the first picture the Buddha gives Queen Vaidehi, the sun hanging in the west like a drum. Your line was the drum in the west.

A bowl of water left out on a winter night. By morning it has gone hard and clear, and when you hold it up, the light comes straight through. Nothing was added. Nothing was taken away. The water simply went still, all the way down. That small, ordinary change is the next step in the meditations of the sutra Pure Land Buddhists call the Contemplation Sutra. After the sun, the queen is shown water, and the water does not stay water for long. Today: water and ice.
screen: `A BOWL OF WATER ON A WINTER NIGHT.` → `BY MORNING, CLEAR ICE.` → `THE NEXT PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, the steps. After the setting sun, the sutra describes a second contemplation. Look at water, and see it clear and pure, so clear the mind does not scatter. Then see the water as ice, shining and transparent. Then let the ice become a ground of jewel, clear inside and out, with light streaming up from beneath it. That ground, the sutra says, is the ground of the land of bliss. Second, why water comes next. A sunset is far away; you can only look at it. Water is something anyone has held in a cupped hand, felt cold, poured out. The picture moves closer. And the water isn't swapped for something else. It changes state, water to ice, ice to jewel, the same clearness carried through each change. Third, the stillness. Water only shows a clear picture when it stops moving, and ice is water that has stopped completely. Some readers hear the mind in this: stirred, it clouds; settled, the light gets through. The sutra itself doesn't spell that out. It simply asks for the picture, held steadily, eyes open or closed. Fourth, how it lives today. Some Pure Land practitioners work through these pictures in order, slowly, one at a time. For others, the name of Amitabha is the center, and the pictures stay in the sutra as a doorway they know is there. Either way, the instruction is the same: one clear picture, held steady.

If the picture ripples or fades, let it settle again, the way water does on its own. If it comes easily, let the water turn to clear ice, and rest there.

1263.title: Calling the name
1263.hook: Namu Amida Butsu in Japan, Namo Amituofo in China
1263.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists say the nembutsu aloud in temple services, quietly in daily life, and with prayer beads to keep count; Japanese practitioners say Namu Amida Butsu, and Chinese practitioners Namo Amituofo.

segments.voice: Yesterday, water and ice: still water turning to shining ice, and the ice to a jewel ground. Your line was clear as water.

In a temple in Kyoto, a room full of voices: Namu Amida Butsu. In a temple in Taipei or Singapore, the same name in another tongue: Namo Amituofo. A grandmother says it over her rice. A monk says it as he passes you in a corridor. A man in a hospital bed says it under his breath when the pain comes. The sutra's pictures take patience. This practice can be done by anyone with a voice, or just the breath to whisper. Today's word is the name, said aloud: nembutsu.
screen: `NAMU AMIDA BUTSU.` → `NAMO AMITUOFO.` → `SAID OVER RICE, IN A CORRIDOR, IN A HOSPITAL BED.`

segments.voice: First, the name, which you met in year three with Honen. Namu Amida Butsu and Namo Amituofo are one phrase in two languages. Amida and Amituofo are both Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light. Namu, or namo, is a word of bowing: homage, turning toward, taking refuge. So the whole phrase is a bow, made of sound. Second, the word nembutsu. It's usually rendered as keeping the Buddha in mind. In Pure Land practice, keeping the Buddha in mind came to include saying his name aloud; thinking and saying grew close enough to share a word. Third, the passage that makes this practice so plain. Near the end of the Contemplation Sutra, the Buddha describes a person who has done much wrong in life and comes to the hour of death in fear and pain. A good friend sits beside him and tries to teach him to picture the Buddha, but he can't; he is too pressed by suffering to hold any picture at all. So the friend says, in effect: if you cannot think of him, just say his name. The sutra says he calls the name ten times, and is born in the land of bliss. Fourth, why that matters. The pictures need a steady mind. The name is offered to the person who has none left. Pure Land teachers who put it at the heart of the path point to this passage: it is within reach on the worst day as on the best.
screen: `ONE NAME IN TWO LANGUAGES.` · `NAMU: A BOW. AMIDA: INFINITE LIGHT.` · `IF YOU CANNOT PICTURE HIM, SAY HIS NAME.` · `WITHIN REACH ON THE WORST DAY.` · then, large: `JUST THE NAME.`

segments.voice: If you'd like, say Namu Amida Butsu or Namo Amituofo slowly, once with each out-breath, ten times, aloud or under your breath, counting on your fingers if that helps. If you'd rather not say it, listen to the sound of it in your mind, as a word from a tradition you're visiting. After the tenth, sit quietly with whatever is left.
Nembutsu. Keeping the Buddha in mind, and in Pure Land practice, calling his name: Namu Amida Butsu, Namo Amituofo. Today's word.
Your line: just the name. When the pictures won't come, the name still can. Rest well.

1264.title: Tanluan and Shandao
1264.hook: the Chinese teachers who shaped Pure Land practice
1264.howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists in China and Japan honor Tanluan and Shandao as teachers of their lineage; in Japanese Shin temples, Shinran's verses naming them are chanted in services, and Shandao's parable of the white path is still taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nembutsu: Namu Amida Butsu, Namo Amituofo, one name in two languages, offered to the one who can't picture anything. Your line was just the name.

A traveler is crossing a wide wasteland, alone, with bandits and wild beasts closing in behind him. Ahead lie two rivers: on the left, a river of fire; on the right, a river of water, waves crashing. Between them runs a white path only a few inches wide, with fire and water licking at it from both sides. From the near bank, a voice: go, take this path. From the far bank, another: come straight here, I will protect you. That story was told by a Chinese teacher, Shandao. Today: two of the teachers in China who shaped how Pure Land is practiced.
screen: `A TRAVELER, CHASED.` → `FIRE ON THE LEFT, WATER ON THE RIGHT.` → `A NARROW WHITE PATH BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: First, Tanluan. Tradition says he started out looking for a long life, studying texts on how to live for ages. Then he met an Indian monk, Bodhiruci, who handed him a Pure Land sutra and said, in effect: here is a life without measure. The story goes that Tanluan burned his books on long life and turned to Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Life. Second, what he taught. His commentary on a treatise about the Pure Land opens with two paths, borrowed from the Indian teacher Nagarjuna. One is like traveling overland on foot, slow and hard. The other is like crossing water in a boat, easy, because something other than your legs carries you. Tanluan leaned his teaching on the power of Amitabha's vow, and tomorrow's word grows out of that. Third, Shandao's white path. The traveler is ordinary life, chased by its dangers. The river of fire is anger; the river of water is craving. The path is narrow, but it's there, and two voices guide it: the Buddha who sends from this shore, and Amitabha who calls from the far one. The traveler steps out, and the parable says he reaches the far bank. Fourth, why these names matter. Shandao urged saying the name with one heart, walking, standing, sitting or lying down. Tradition says that line, read in Japan by Honen, turned him to the nembutsu. And Shinran named both Tanluan and Shandao among the teachers of his line.

1265.title: Other power
1265.hook: Shinran: awakening comes through Amida's power, not our own effort
1265.howItsDone: In Jodo Shinshu, Shin Buddhists understand birth in the Pure Land as the work of Amida's vow, other power, rather than their own effort; they say the nembutsu, and hear Shinran's teaching in temple talks and in readings from the Tannisho.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tanluan and Shandao: the books on long life burned, the white path between fire and water. Your line was the Chinese masters.

A monk comes down a mountain. Tradition says Shinran spent long years training on Mount Hiei, the monastery mountain above Kyoto, with study, chanting and long nights of practice, and came down convinced that none of it had changed what was wrong inside him. In the city he found Honen, the teacher of the nembutsu, and stayed. A disciple wrote down what Shinran said about that choice: even if Honen had misled him, and saying the name led him to hell, he would have no regret, because no other practice had ever been within his reach. Today's word is what he was leaning on: tariki.
screen: `A MONK COMES DOWN THE MOUNTAIN.` → `HE FINDS HONEN.` → `NO OTHER PRACTICE WAS WITHIN REACH.`

segments.voice: First, two words, building on the Shinran you met in year three. Jiriki means self power: awakening built by your own effort, your discipline, your merit. Tariki means other power: the power of Amida's vow, working on you from outside your own effort. Yesterday the easy path was Tanluan's boat. Tariki is the boat. Second, what Shinran did with it. For him, other power reaches all the way down. Not only is the Pure Land Amida's gift; even the trust that receives it, even the nembutsu on your lips, is Amida at work, not a technique you perform well. Third, the line people stop at. The same record of his words, the Tannisho, has him say: even a good person is born in the Pure Land, so how much more an evil person. The record's explanation: the person who trusts their own goodness still leans, a little, on self power. The one who knows they have nothing to offer leans entirely on the vow. Fourth, what it is not. Other power is no excuse to stop caring how you live; the record has Shinran warning against people who did wrong on purpose, thinking the vow would cover it. And Pure Land teachers differ here. In Honen's Jodo school, the nembutsu is practiced often and earnestly, as the practice the vow chose. In Shinran's Jodo Shinshu, the emphasis falls on receiving, not achieving. Both say the name; they place the effort differently. What Shinran found coming down the mountain was not a better method. It was the end of needing one.

1266.title: True entrusting
1266.hook: faith as entrusting oneself, not as belief forced by effort
1266.howItsDone: In Jodo Shinshu, shinjin is understood as the entrusting heart given by Amida; Shin Buddhists hear it explained in temple talks and readings from Shinran and the Tannisho, and say the nembutsu as its expression rather than as a way to produce it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tariki: Shinran coming down the mountain and leaning on the power of Amida's vow. Your line was other power.

A disciple brings his teacher an awkward confession. When I say the nembutsu, he says, I don't feel joy leaping up inside me the way I'm told I should. And I'm in no hurry at all to go to the Pure Land. What's wrong with me? A teacher could scold him, or tell him to try harder. In the record called the Tannisho, the disciple is Yuien, the teacher is Shinran, and Shinran answers: I have wondered the very same thing. Today's word is what Shinran says is still there, under the missing joy: shinjin.

segments.voice: First, the word. Shinjin is often translated faith, but in English faith can sound like believing something hard enough, gripping a claim with your will. Some Shin translators render shinjin as true entrusting instead. Not gripping: letting yourself be held. Second, where it comes from. For Shinran, shinjin is not something you produce. Following other power all the way through, he taught that the entrusting heart is itself given by Amida, the Buddha's own mind awakened in an ordinary one. You can't force it into being, any more than you can force yourself to fall asleep. Third, back to Yuien's confession. In the Tannisho, Shinran says the missing joy is the work of our cravings and passions, the very things that hold us back. Then he turns it around: the vow was made precisely for people like this. If we felt nothing but eager joy, we might wonder whether we had any passions left at all. The doubt doesn't disqualify the disciple. It shows him who the vow is for. Fourth, what entrusting looks like. One way to picture it: a child who has stopped fighting sleep in the back seat on a long drive. The child isn't believing hard that the driver is good. The child has simply stopped keeping watch. That letting go isn't lazy; it's a kind of honesty about who is really driving. Shinjin, in Shinran's teaching, is not a feeling to work up. It's a weight finally set down.

1267.title: Gratitude
1267.hook: in Jodo Shinshu, the nembutsu is said as thanks rather than as a technique
1267.howItsDone: In Jodo Shinshu, Shin Buddhists say Namu Amida Butsu as an expression of gratitude for Amida's vow rather than as a practice to earn birth, and sing Shinran's hymns, including one on gratitude, in temple services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shinjin: true entrusting, Yuien's missing joy, and Shinran's I have wondered the same. Your line was entrusted.

Someone ahead of you in line pays for your coffee and walks out before you can say a word. The cup is already in your hand; there's nothing left to earn. You could chase them down the street with exact change, but that would turn a gift into a debt. Or you could stand there, a little surprised, and say thank you, even to an empty doorway. Same words, different job. One is paying. The other is answering. Shin Buddhists make that same distinction about the name itself. Today: gratitude.
screen: `THE COFFEE IS ALREADY PAID FOR.` → `PAYING, OR ANSWERING?` → `THE SAME NAME, A DIFFERENT JOB.`

segments.voice: First, the shift. Earlier this week the nembutsu came to a dying man as the one thing he could still do. In Jodo Shinshu, Shinran's tradition, the name takes on a different job. If birth in the Pure Land is settled by shinjin, the entrusting that Amida gives, then the nembutsu isn't needed to earn anything. It is said afterward, as a response: Namu Amida Butsu becomes a thank-you. Second, the phrase Shin Buddhists use for this: hoon kansha, which they gloss as responding to the Buddha's kindness with gratitude. Not a technique, not a ladder to climb, not a count to keep. Third, where you can hear it. Shinran wrote hymns in plain Japanese, and one of them, on gratitude for Amida's compassion and the kindness of the teachers who passed it on, is sung in Shin temples. The thanks reaches back along the line: to Amida, to Shandao and Tanluan, to Honen, to whoever first said the name to you. Fourth, the week, looking back. It began at the setting sun and the drum in the west. Then clear water and ice. Then the name, for the one who could no longer picture anything. Then the Chinese masters, other power, entrusting. Each day took a little more of the work out of your hands. Gratitude is what's left when the work is gone: the cup already warm, and nothing to say but thanks.
screen: `NOT TO EARN: SAID AFTERWARD.` · `HOON KANSHA: GRATITUDE FOR KINDNESS.` · `THANKS ALONG THE LINE OF TEACHERS.` · `THE WEEK: LESS WORK, MORE THANKS.` · then, large: `SAID IN THANKS.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, say thank you, aloud or silently, ten times: not a tally, just enough to get the thanks moving. Let each one land on something real, the breath, the roof over you, someone who cooked for you, someone who taught you to read; if you say the nembutsu, let it carry the thanks instead. If you lose count, let it go, and when the thanks run quiet, rest with whatever is left.
Gratitude. In Jodo Shinshu, the spirit in which the nembutsu is said: not to earn birth, but in thanks for what Amida has already given. Today's word.
Your line: said in thanks. An answer, not a payment. A week of the name, complete.
